name: Fern
lede: Fern is a clear mid-bright leaf green, and an irony of dye history: ferns were among the plants northern Europeans used to dye green, yet gave weak, unstable results.

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: Our library takes Fern from the xkcd survey, from ISCC-NBS (block 120) and from Maerz and Paul, who date the name to 1924 and place it on plate 21, block I 7 [1]. Its nearest named color is Asparagus [1]. It is lighter and livelier than [[fern-green]], the deeper #4F7942 [2]. Compare [[leaf-green]] and [[apple-green]].

sections.title: Ferns in the dye vat
sections.body:
In northern Europe, Pastoureau notes, green dyeing was relatively easy: nettle, fern, plantain, oak leaves and birch bark gave a wide range of shades [3]. But the dyes hardly penetrated the fibers, and most greens were neither vivid nor solid [3]. For a long time Europeans could not get a pure, rich and stable green from such plants [4].

The same lack of an effective mordant, Pastoureau argues, made the yellows of the so-called barbarian dyers dull and washed out, and fern was one of their sources there too [5].

sections.title: Wearing the May
sections.body: Green was also worn raw. To wear the May meant attaching an element of greenery to oneself, a crown, a necklace or a hat of plants, ferns or branches [6]. Someone seen with no green at all was said to be *pris sans verd* [6].

sections.title: Ash
sections.body: Fern's other contribution was ash. Native American tribesmen mixed burned fern ash into tattoo pigments [7]. Three hundred years ago, Finlay writes, linen workers near Glasgow bleached cloth with sour milk and fern ashes, laying it out in lines for many days [8].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, only 6 (0.03%) hold this swatch within six units of ΔE2000 over at least five per cent of the canvas, as photographed [9]. The strongest is a *Portrait of Emperor Jahangir*, 1795, where it covers 32% of the picture [9]. Next come Matisse's *Nymph and Satyr*, 1908, Gauguin's *Mother and Child under a Tree at Pont-Aven*, 1886, and Van Gogh's [[painting:nga-163323|Green Wheat Fields, Auvers]], 1890, at 16% [9].

Five of the six date from 1886 or later [9]. The clear mid-green that fern could not give a dyer is rare in old painting, and these few matches are mostly from the modern era. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is not a pigment test.

choices: The dyes hardly penetrated the fibers, so greens were not vivid or solid

openers: Ferns were a dye plant for green in northern Europe, but never a good one [3].
Only 6 of 23,781 museum paintings hold this clear mid-green, and five of them date from 1886 or later [9].
